deep.reconstruction:
Context. The page belongs to Grothendieck's 1983-84 notes on systems of pseudolines in the (topological) projective plane X. The previous page builds a cell complex X̃ attached to a fixed arrangement. A moving ('variable') pseudoline D is classified by its position relative to the arrangement:
- stable (generic) positions give the faces;
- semi-stable positions give the edges;
- critical positions, where D passes through a vertex of the arrangement, give the vertices.
Oriented versions and involutions σ act on X̃. 'Repères' (D, s, ω, σ̄) are flag-like data: a critical D, a vertex s on it, an orientation ω of D, and a local orientation σ̄ of X at s.

This page (drawn on the back of a 1982 Cray CFT Fortran listing, 'PROGRAM CRAY7 … BONJOUR') works out a concrete closed path P_f in X̃.

The drawings. Orange strokes are arrangement pseudolines crossing in X-shaped vertices. Two of them are drawn as a big orange arc joining two crossing points, which are identified (s6 = s1): this is the projective closing-up. The dark-green and light-green curves are successive positions of the moving pseudoline D. The dashed brown polygonal line joins the vertices s1, …, s5 (top) and t2, t3 (bottom) in the order D meets them. In the lower large figure, blue numerals 1–19 record the order in which the vertices are swept.

The path P_f. It is the sequence of positions D1, …, D20, each passage through a vertex being an elementary move (a 'flip' across a vertex). It is grouped by vertical bars into blocks:
- D1 | D2…D6 meets s1 … s5, s6 = s1;
- D7…D13 meets s2, t2, s3, s4, t3, s5, s6 = s1;
- D14…D20 meets s2, t2, s3(?), s4, t3, s5, s6 = s1.
The question D20 =? D6 asks whether the path closes up, i.e. returns to the same cell.

The periodicity check. The note 'D18 = D4 → D19 = D5' and the top-right enlarged figure check whether positions three steps apart in the period coincide combinatorially. The figure shows two positions D4 (dark) and D18 (light) of the moving line, with labels s4 (4) and t3 (18), between two pairs of orange lines. They are drawn as crossing twice, forming a lens; the labels D1 = D19 and D5 = D19 (faint) are written near them. The '5=19 !' suggests Grothendieck found an identification of cells, possibly unexpected, closing the loop.

Smaller figures. These show a local repère: a vertex with orientation arrows ω, ϖ, and a green D. One is annotated 'rive sans passage' (bank/shore without passage), apparently a region boundary that D cannot cross without passing a vertex.

Purpose. To understand the topology of the space of pseudolines extending a given arrangement, i.e. the complex X̃, and its loops. Concretely, he computes a non-trivial closed sweep of a pseudoline around the projective plane through all vertices and checks its periodicity.
errors: The machine transcription's third block reads 's_2, t_2, t_3, s_4, t_3, s_5'. The image more plausibly reads 's_2, t_2, s_3 (written over), s_4, t_3, s_5'. With that reading blocks 2 and 3 are identical. That fits D18 = D4, D19 = D5 (period 14 counted from block 1 to block 3). As transcribed, t3 would occur twice in one block, which is impossible for a single sweep.

Two distinct pseudolines in the projective plane cross exactly once. Read literally, the drawn double crossing of D4 and D18 is therefore not two pseudolines of one arrangement. It must be read as two positions of the moving line (different cells, or the same cell up to isotopy). The page does not settle this; the '=' and '?' marks show the identification was itself being tested.
D20 =? D6 is left with a question mark. Whether the loop closes is not decided on this page.

ideas.what: Cell complex of positions of a moving pseudoline relative to a fixed arrangement: stable / semi-stable / critical positions as faces / edges / vertices
ideas.modern_name: Extension space (space of one-element extensions) of a rank-3 oriented matroid; topological representation via Levi's enlargement lemma
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926); Sturmfels–Ziegler, 'Extension spaces of oriented matroids' (1993); Mnëv–Ziegler

ideas.what: A moving pseudoline sweeping through all vertices of the arrangement, one flip at a time, recorded as an ordered sequence of vertices/positions
ideas.modern_name: Topological sweep / allowable sequences / sweeps of pseudoline arrangements

ideas.what: Closing a sweep around the projective plane (s6 = s1) and asking whether the sequence of cells is periodic (D20 =? D6, D18 = D4, D19 = D5)
ideas.modern_name: Closed loops / periodic sweeps in the extension space; half-period phenomenon of allowable sequences in the projective plane

ideas.what: Repère = (critical D, vertex s, orientation ω of D, local orientation of X at s), used as oriented edges of X̃
ideas.modern_name: Flags / oriented local frames in a regular cell complex (a barycentric/flag-complex viewpoint)

missed.claim: Grothendieck explicitly computes a closed loop in his complex X̃ of positions of a variable pseudoline and questions its periodicity. Read with the previous page, this is a hands-on study of the topology (loops, involutions) of the extension space of a pseudoline arrangement, roughly a decade before Sturmfels–Ziegler. The thread (D20 =? D6) is left open on this page.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Extension spaces of rank-3 oriented matroids, and their homotopy type, are a known topic. An independent early cellular model with orientation involutions could be of historical interest. Mathematically it is likely subsumed by existing results.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a worked example: a periodic sweep of a pseudoline around a projective arrangement inside a cell complex of positions. The ideas are close to known notions (allowable sequences, topological sweep, extension spaces), and nothing here is a finished new result. Mild interest lies in Grothendieck's independent cellular viewpoint, and in the historical detail that the notes are written on a 1982 Cray Fortran printout.
transcription_corrections: Third vertex block likely reads 's_2, t_2, s_3, s_4, t_3, s_5' (the third item is an overwritten s_3), not 's_2, t_2, t_3, s_4, t_3, s_5'.
'S = 19 !' at right of top figure should read '5 = 19 !' (i.e. D_5 = D_19).
Top-right label reads 'D_1 = D_19' (possibly D_1 =? D_19); the faint lower label is 'D_5 = D_19'.
'rive sans passage' near the lower-left small figure appears correct; the word below is illegible (possibly 'passage' repeated).
'pr. s. o.' is uncertain; it is possibly an abbreviation for an oriented stable position ('position stable orientée').
